# base64 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64/^0.22/

## Expand description

Correct, fast, and configurable [base64](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Base64) decoding and encoding. Base64
transports binary data efficiently in contexts where only plain text is
allowed.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Use an [ Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html) to decode or encode base64, configured with the base64
alphabet and padding behavior best suited to your application.

[§](https://docs.rs#engine-setup)Engine setup

There is more than one way to encode a stream of bytes as “base64”.
Different applications use different encoding
[alphabets](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) and
[padding behaviors](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurposeConfig.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-alphabet)Encoding alphabet

Almost all base64 [alphabets](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) use `A-Z`, `a-z`, and
`0-9`, which gives nearly 64 characters (26 + 26 + 10 = 62), but they differ
in their choice of their final 2.

Most applications use the [standard](https://docs.rs/alphabet/constant.STANDARD.html) alphabet specified
in [RFC 4648](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-4).  If that’s all you need, you can get started
quickly by using the pre-configured
[ STANDARD](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.STANDARD.html) engine, which is also available
in the

[module as shown here, if you prefer a minimal](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude``use`
footprint.```
use base64::prelude::*;
assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.decode(b"+uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "/+wgVQA=");
```
Other common alphabets are available in the [ alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/index.html) module.

[§](https://docs.rs#url-safe-alphabet)URL-safe alphabet

The standard alphabet uses `+` and `/` as its two non-alphanumeric tokens,
which cannot be safely used in URL’s without encoding them as `%2B` and
`%2F`.

To avoid that, some applications use a [“URL-safe” alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/constant.URL_SAFE.html),
which uses `-` and `_` instead. To use that alternative alphabet, use the
[ URL_SAFE](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.URL_SAFE.html) engine. This example doesn’t
use

[to show what a more explicit](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude``use` would look like.```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::URL_SAFE, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.decode(b"-uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "_-wgVQA=");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#padding-characters)Padding characters

Each base64 character represents 6 bits (2⁶ = 64) of the original binary data, and every 3 bytes of input binary data will encode to 4 base64 characters (8 bits × 3 = 6 bits × 4 = 24 bits).

When the input is not an even multiple of 3 bytes in length, [canonical](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-3.5)
base64 encoders insert padding characters at the end, so that the output
length is always a multiple of 4:

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b""),    "");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg==");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8=");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
```
Canonical encoding ensures that base64 encodings will be exactly the same,
byte-for-byte, regardless of input length. But the `=` padding characters
aren’t necessary for decoding, and they may be omitted by using a
[ NO_PAD](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.NO_PAD.html) configuration:

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD_NO_PAD, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b""),    "");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
```
The pre-configured `NO_PAD` engines will reject inputs containing padding
`=` characters. To encode without padding and still accept padding while
decoding, create an [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) with
that [padding mode](https://docs.rs/engine/enum.DecodePaddingMode.html).

`assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.decode(b"Zm8="), Err(base64::DecodeError::InvalidPadding));`[§](https://docs.rs#further-customization)Further customization

Decoding and encoding behavior can be customized by creating an
[engine](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) with an [alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) and
[padding configuration](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurposeConfig.html):

```
use base64::{engine, alphabet, Engine as _};
// bizarro-world base64: +/ as the first symbols instead of the last
let alphabet =
    alphabet::Alphabet::new("+/ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789")
    .unwrap();
// a very weird config that encodes with padding but requires no padding when decoding...?
let crazy_config = engine::GeneralPurposeConfig::new()
    .with_decode_allow_trailing_bits(true)
    .with_encode_padding(true)
    .with_decode_padding_mode(engine::DecodePaddingMode::RequireNone);
let crazy_engine = engine::GeneralPurpose::new(&alphabet, crazy_config);
let encoded = crazy_engine.encode(b"abc 123");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#memory-allocation)Memory allocation

The [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and [encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) engine methods
allocate memory for their results – `decode` returns a `Vec<u8>` and
`encode` returns a `String`. To instead decode or encode into a buffer that
you allocated, use one of the alternative methods:

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding)Decoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::decode` | returns a new `Vec<u8>` | always |
| `Engine::decode_vec` | appends to provided `Vec<u8>` | if `Vec`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::decode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding)Encoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::encode` | returns a new `String` | always |
| `Engine::encode_string` | appends to provided `String` | if `String`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::encode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#input-and-output)Input and output

The `base64` crate can [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and
[encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) values in memory, or
[ DecoderReader](https://docs.rs/read/struct.DecoderReader.html) and

[provide streaming decoding and encoding for any](https://docs.rs/write/struct.EncoderWriter.html)

`EncoderWriter`[readable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html)or

[writable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)byte stream.

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding-1)Decoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, read::DecoderReader};
let mut input = io::stdin();
let mut decoder = DecoderReader::new(&mut input, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut decoder, &mut io::stdout())?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-1)Encoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, write::EncoderWriter};
let mut output = io::stdout();
let mut encoder = EncoderWriter::new(&mut output, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut io::stdin(), &mut encoder)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#display)Display

If you only need a base64 representation for implementing the
[ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) trait, use

[:](https://docs.rs/display/struct.Base64Display.html)

`Base64Display````
use base64::{display::Base64Display, engine::general_purpose::STANDARD};
let value = Base64Display::new(b"\0\x01\x02\x03", &STANDARD);
assert_eq!("base64: AAECAw==", format!("base64: {}", value));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If length calculations result in overflowing `usize`, a panic will result.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use engine::`- [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/index.html)
- Provides [Alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html)and constants for alphabets commonly used in the wild.
- [display](https://docs.rs/display/index.html)
- Enables base64’d output anywhere you might use a `Display`implementation, like a format string.
- [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/index.html)
- Provides the [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html)abstraction and out of the box implementations.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Preconfigured engines for common use cases.
- [read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html)
- Implementations of `io::Read`to transparently decode base64.
- [write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html)
- Implementations of `io::Write`to transparently handle base64.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Decode](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html)- Error
- Errors that can occur while decoding.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeSliceError.html)- Slice - Error
- Errors that can occur while decoding into a slice.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/enum.EncodeSliceError.html)- Slice - Error

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode](https://docs.rs/fn.decode.html)- Deprecated
- Decode base64 using the `STANDARD`engine
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine.html)- engine - Deprecated
- Decode from string reference as octets using the specified [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html).
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine_slice.html)- engine_ - slice - Deprecated
- Decode the input into the provided output slice.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine_vec.html)- engine_ - vec - Deprecated
- Decode from string reference as octets.
- [decoded_](https://docs.rs/fn.decoded_len_estimate.html)- len_ - estimate
- Returns a conservative estimate of the decoded size of `encoded_len`base64 symbols (rounded up to the next group of 3 decoded bytes).
- [encode](https://docs.rs/fn.encode.html)- Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 using the `STANDARD`engine
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine.html)- engine - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 using the provided `Engine`into a new`String`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine_slice.html)- engine_ - slice - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 into a supplied slice.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine_string.html)- engine_ - string - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 into a supplied `String`.
- [encoded_](https://docs.rs/fn.encoded_len.html)- len
- Calculate the base64 encoded length for a given input length, optionally including any appropriate padding bytes.

# http - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/http/^1/

## Expand description

A general purpose library of common HTTP types

This crate is a general purpose library for common types found when working
with the HTTP protocol. You’ll find [ Request](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html) and

[types for working as either a client or a server as well as all of their components. Notably you’ll find](https://docs.rs/response/struct.Response.html)

`Response``Uri` for what a [is requesting, a](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html)

`Request`[for how it’s being requested, a](https://docs.rs/method/struct.Method.html)

`Method`[for what sort of response came back, a](https://docs.rs/status/struct.StatusCode.html)

`StatusCode`[for how this was communicated, and](https://docs.rs/version/struct.Version.html)

`Version`[/](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderName.html)

`HeaderName`[definitions to get grouped in a](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderValue.html)

`HeaderValue`[to work with request/response headers.](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderMap.html)

`HeaderMap`You will notably *not* find an implementation of sending requests or
spinning up a server in this crate. It’s intended that this crate is the
“standard library” for HTTP clients and servers without dictating any
particular implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#requests-and-responses)Requests and Responses

Perhaps the main two types in this crate are the [ Request](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html) and

[types. A](https://docs.rs/response/struct.Response.html)

`Response`[could either be constructed to get sent off as a client or it can also be received to generate a](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html)

`Request`[for a server. Similarly as a client a](https://docs.rs/response/struct.Response.html)

`Response`[is what you get after sending a](https://docs.rs/response/struct.Response.html)

`Response`[, whereas on a server you’ll be manufacturing a](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html)

`Request`[to send back to the client.](https://docs.rs/response/struct.Response.html)

`Response`Each type has a number of accessors for the component fields. For as a server you might want to inspect a requests URI to dispatch it:

```
use http::{Request, Response};
fn response(req: Request<()>) -> http::Result<Response<()>> {
    match req.uri().path() {
        "/" => index(req),
        "/foo" => foo(req),
        "/bar" => bar(req),
        _ => not_found(req),
    }
}
```
On a [ Request](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html) you’ll also find accessors like

[to return a](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html#method.method)

`method`[and](https://docs.rs/method/struct.Method.html)

`Method`[to inspect the various headers. A](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html#method.method)

`headers`[has similar methods for headers, the status code, etc.](https://docs.rs/response/struct.Response.html)

`Response`In addition to getters, request/response types also have mutable accessors to edit the request/response:

```
use http::{HeaderValue, Response, StatusCode};
use http::header::CONTENT_TYPE;
fn add_server_headers<T>(response: &mut Response<T>) {
    response.headers_mut()
        .insert(CONTENT_TYPE, HeaderValue::from_static("text/html"));
    *response.status_mut() = StatusCode::OK;
}
```
And finally, one of the most important aspects of requests/responses, the
body! The [ Request](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html) and

[types in this crate are](https://docs.rs/response/struct.Response.html)

`Response`*generic*in what their body is. This allows downstream libraries to use different representations such as

`Request<Vec<u8>>`, `Response<impl Read>`,
`Request<impl Stream<Item = Vec<u8>, Error = _>>`, or even
`Response<MyCustomType>` where the custom type was deserialized from JSON.The body representation is intentionally flexible to give downstream libraries maximal flexibility in implementing the body as appropriate.

[§](https://docs.rs#http-headers)HTTP Headers

Another major piece of functionality in this library is HTTP header
interpretation and generation. The `HeaderName` type serves as a way to
define header *names*, or what’s to the left of the colon. A `HeaderValue`
conversely is the header *value*, or what’s to the right of a colon.

For example, if you have an HTTP request that looks like:

```
GET /foo HTTP/1.1
Accept: text/html
```
Then `"Accept"` is a [ HeaderName](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderName.html) while

`"text/html"` is a [. Each of these is a dedicated type to allow for a number of interesting optimizations and to also encode the static guarantees of each type. For example a](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderValue.html)

`HeaderValue`[is always a valid](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderName.html)

`HeaderName``&str`, but a [may not be valid UTF-8.](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderValue.html)

`HeaderValue`The most common header names are already defined for you as constant values
in the [ header](https://docs.rs/header/index.html) module of this crate. For example:

```
use http::header::{self, HeaderName};
let name: HeaderName = header::ACCEPT;
assert_eq!(name.as_str(), "accept");
```
You can, however, also parse header names from strings:

```
use http::header::{self, HeaderName};
let name = "Accept".parse::<HeaderName>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(name, header::ACCEPT);
```
Header values can be created from string literals through the [ from_static](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderValue.html#method.from_static)
function:

```
use http::HeaderValue;
let value = HeaderValue::from_static("text/html");
assert_eq!(value.as_bytes(), b"text/html");
```
And header values can also be parsed like names:

```
use http::HeaderValue;
let value = "text/html";
let value = value.parse::<HeaderValue>().unwrap();
```
Most HTTP requests and responses tend to come with more than one header, so
it’s not too useful to just work with names and values only! This crate also
provides a [ HeaderMap](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderMap.html) type which is a specialized hash map for keys as

[and generic values. This type, like header names, is optimized for common usage but should continue to scale with your needs over time.](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderName.html)

`HeaderName`[§](https://docs.rs#uris)URIs

Each HTTP [ Request](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html) has an associated URI with it. This may just be a path
like

`/index.html` but it could also be an absolute URL such as
`https://www.rust-lang.org/index.html`. A [has a number of accessors to interpret it:](https://docs.rs/uri/struct.Uri.html)

`URI````
use http::Uri;
use http::uri::Scheme;
let uri = "https://www.rust-lang.org/index.html".parse::<Uri>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(uri.scheme(), Some(&Scheme::HTTPS));
assert_eq!(uri.host(), Some("www.rust-lang.org"));
assert_eq!(uri.path(), "/index.html");
assert_eq!(uri.query(), None);
```

- `pub use crate::header::`- [HeaderName](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderName.html);

# rmcp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rmcp/^1.6/

## Expand description

The official Rust SDK for the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25). Build MCP servers that expose tools, resources, and prompts to AI assistants — or build clients that connect to them.

For **getting started**, **usage guides**, and **full MCP feature documentation** (resources, prompts, sampling, roots, logging, completions, subscriptions, etc.), see the [main README](https://docs.rs/README.md).

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

| Feature | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `server` | Server functionality and the tool system | ✅ |
| `client` | Client functionality | |
| `macros` | `#[tool]`/`#[prompt]`macros (re-exports)`rmcp-macros` | ✅ |
| `schemars` | JSON Schema generation for tool definitions | |
| `auth` | OAuth 2.0 authentication support | |
| `elicitation` | Elicitation support |

[§](https://docs.rs#transport-features)Transport features

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| `transport-io` | Server-side stdio transport |
| `transport-child-process` | Client-side stdio transport (spawns a child process) |
| `transport-async-rw` | Generic async read/write transport |
| `transport-streamable-http-client` | Streamable HTTP client (transport-agnostic) |
| `transport-streamable-http-client-reqwest` | Streamable HTTP client with default `reqwest`backend |
| `transport-streamable-http-server` | Streamable HTTP server transport |

[§](https://docs.rs#tls-backend-options-for-http-transports)TLS backend options (for HTTP transports)

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| `reqwest` | Uses rustls — pure Rust TLS (recommended default) |
| `reqwest-native-tls` | Uses platform-native TLS (OpenSSL / Secure Transport / SChannel) |
| `reqwest-tls-no-provider` | Uses rustls without a default crypto provider (bring your own) |

[§](https://docs.rs#transports)Transports

The transport layer is pluggable. Two built-in pairs cover the most common cases:

| Client | Server | |
|---|---|---|
| stdio | `TokioChildProcess` | `stdio` |
| Streamable HTTP | `StreamableHttpClientTransport` | `StreamableHttpService` |

Any type that implements the [ Transport](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html) trait can be used. The

[helper trait provides automatic conversions from:](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.IntoTransport.html)

`IntoTransport`- `(Sink, Stream)`or a combined- `Sink + Stream`
- `(AsyncRead, AsyncWrite)`or a combined- `AsyncRead + AsyncWrite`
- A `Worker`
- A `Transport`

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

This project is licensed under the terms specified in the repository’s [LICENSE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE) file.

# thiserror - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/thiserror/^2/

## Expand description

This library provides a convenient derive macro for the standard library’s
[ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/error/trait.Error.html) trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use thiserror::Error;
#[derive(Error, Debug)]
pub enum DataStoreError {
    #[error("data store disconnected")]
    Disconnect(#[from] io::Error),
    #[error("the data for key `{0}` is not available")]
    Redaction(String),
    #[error("invalid header (expected {expected:?}, found {found:?})")]
    InvalidHeader {
        expected: String,
        found: String,
    },
    #[error("unknown data store error")]
    Unknown,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

-
Thiserror deliberately does not appear in your public API. You get the same thing as if you had written an implementation of `std::error::Error`
-
Errors may be enums, structs with named fields, tuple structs, or unit structs.
-
A `Display``#[error("...")]`messages on the struct or each variant of your enum, as shown above in the example.The messages support a shorthand for interpolating fields from the error. - `#[error("{var}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.0)`
- `#[error("{var:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.0)`
 These shorthands can be used together with any additional format args, which may be arbitrary expressions. For example: `#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("invalid rdo_lookahead_frames {0} (expected < {max})", max = i32::MAX)] InvalidLookahead(u32), }`If one of the additional expression arguments needs to refer to a field of the struct or enum, then refer to named fields as `.var`and tuple fields as`.0`.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("first letter must be lowercase but was {:?}", first_char(.0))] WrongCase(String), #[error("invalid index {idx}, expected at least {} and at most {}", .limits.lo, .limits.hi)] OutOfBounds { idx: usize, limits: Limits }, }`
-
A `From``#[from]`attribute.The variant using `#[from]`must not contain any other fields beyond the source error (and possibly a backtrace — see below). Usually`#[from]`fields are unnamed, but`#[from]`is allowed on a named field too.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io(#[from] io::Error), Glob(#[from] globset::Error), }`
-
The Error trait’s `source()``#[source]`attribute or is named`source`, if any. This is for identifying the underlying lower level error that caused your error.The `#[from]`attribute always implies that the same field is`#[source]`, so you don’t ever need to specify both attributes.Any error type that implements `std::error::Error`or dereferences to`dyn std::error::Error`will work as a source.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, #[source] // optional if field name is `source` source: anyhow::Error, }`
-
The Error trait’s `provide()``Backtrace`, if any, as a`std::backtrace::Backtrace``Backtrace`in errors requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`use std::backtrace::Backtrace; #[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, backtrace: Backtrace, // automatically detected }`
-
If a field is both a source (named `source`, or has`#[source]`or`#[from]`attribute)*and*is marked`#[backtrace]`, then the Error trait’s`provide()``provide`so that both layers of the error share the same backtrace. The`#[backtrace]`attribute requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[backtrace] source: io::Error, }, }`
-
For variants that use `#[from]`and also contain a`Backtrace`field, a backtrace is captured from within the`From`impl.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[from] source: io::Error, backtrace: Backtrace, }, }`
-
Errors may use `error(transparent)`to forward the source and`Display``#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { ... #[error(transparent)] Other(#[from] anyhow::Error), // source and Display delegate to anyhow::Error }`Another use case is hiding implementation details of an error representation behind an opaque error type, so that the representation is able to evolve without breaking the crate’s public API. `// PublicError is public, but opaque and easy to keep compatible. #[derive(Error, Debug)] #[error(transparent)] pub struct PublicError(#[from] ErrorRepr); impl PublicError { // Accessors for anything we do want to expose publicly. } // Private and free to change across minor version of the crate. #[derive(Error, Debug)] enum ErrorRepr { ... }`
-
See also the `anyhow`

---

# lash_plugin_mcp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lash-plugin-mcp/0.1.0-alpha.82/target-redirect/lash_plugin_mcp/

## Expand description

MCP (Model Context Protocol) integration for `lash`, packaged as a plugin.

`lash-plugin-mcp` exposes MCP-compatible servers as a normal lash tool
provider. Add the plugin once at [`LashCore::builder`] time, supply a
`BTreeMap<String, McpServerConfig>`, and every session built from the
core gets the configured servers’ tools surfaced under
`mcp__<server>__<tool>` names.

Supported transports (selected per server via the `transport` field):

- `stdio`— spawn a child process and speak JSON-RPC over its pipes.
- `streamable_http`— HTTP/JSON streaming transport (newer MCP spec).
- `sse`— older HTTP+SSE transport.

Implementation note: the wire-level client is provided by the official
[ rmcp](https://docs.rs/rmcp/1.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rmcp/index.html) SDK. The plugin owns a single connection pool (

`McpConnectionPool`)
that is shared across every session built from the same `LashCore`, so
e.g. stdio servers are spawned once per process rather than per session.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use config::`- [McpServerConfig](https://docs.rs/config/enum.McpServerConfig.html);
- `pub use error::`- [McpError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.McpError.html);
- `pub use plugin::`- [McpDeferredToolProvider](https://docs.rs/plugin/struct.McpDeferredToolProvider.html);
- `pub use plugin::`- [McpPluginFactory](https://docs.rs/plugin/struct.McpPluginFactory.html);
- `pub use plugin::`- [McpToolProvider](https://docs.rs/plugin/struct.McpToolProvider.html);
- `pub use pool::`- [McpConnectionPool](https://docs.rs/pool/struct.McpConnectionPool.html);
- `pub use pool::`- [McpServerStatus](https://docs.rs/pool/struct.McpServerStatus.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- [naming](https://docs.rs/naming/index.html)
- Tool name prefixing helpers. Moved verbatim from `crates/lash/src/mcp.rs`so the`mcp__<server>__<tool>`naming scheme keeps producing identical names (avoids breaking config files / saved trajectories that reference tools by their full prefixed name).
- [plugin](https://docs.rs/plugin/index.html)
- `PluginFactory`- `LashCore`.
- [pool](https://docs.rs/pool/index.html)
- Per-core MCP connection pool.

[§](https://docs.rs#transports)Transports

The transport layer is pluggable. Two built-in pairs cover the most common cases:

| Client | Server | |
|---|---|---|
| stdio | `TokioChildProcess` | `stdio` |
| Streamable HTTP | `StreamableHttpClientTransport` | `StreamableHttpService` |

Any type that implements the [ Transport](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html) trait can be used. The

[helper trait provides automatic conversions from:](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.IntoTransport.html)

`IntoTransport`- `(Sink, Stream)`or a combined- `Sink + Stream`
- `(AsyncRead, AsyncWrite)`or a combined- `AsyncRead + AsyncWrite`
- A `Worker`
- A `Transport`

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

This project is licensed under the terms specified in the repository’s [LICENSE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE) file.

Errors surfaced by `lash-plugin-mcp` when a server fails to connect,
when a tool call errors out, or when the registry rejects the new
surface.

# McpDeferredToolProvider in lash_plugin_mcp::plugin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lash-plugin-mcp/0.1.0-alpha.82/lash_plugin_mcp/plugin/struct.McpDeferredToolProvider.html

`pub struct McpDeferredToolProvider { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Non-resident MCP provider for RLM deferred execution.

It advertises no catalog members, but resolves and executes known MCP tools by id for explicit deferred grants.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# McpPluginFactory in lash_plugin_mcp::plugin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lash-plugin-mcp/0.1.0-alpha.82/lash_plugin_mcp/plugin/struct.McpPluginFactory.html

`pub struct McpPluginFactory { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Plugin factory for MCP. Add once to `LashCoreBuilder` via
`.plugin(Arc::new(factory))`.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Connect to every configured server and return a factory whose pool is
ready to use. Servers are tried eagerly, but one being down never
fails construction — the pool keeps reconnecting in the background and
the server’s tools become available once it comes up. Only
configuration errors fail. The pool is `Arc`-shared across sessions;
cloning the factory and adding it to multiple `LashCore`s shares the
same connections.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lash_plugin_mcp/plugin.rs.html#49-51)#### pub fn [pool](https://docs.rs#method.pool)(&self) -> &[Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<[McpConnectionPool](https://docs.rs/pool/struct.McpConnectionPool.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lash_plugin_mcp/plugin.rs.html#49-51)

#### pub fn [pool](https://docs.rs#method.pool)(&self) -> &[Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<[McpConnectionPool](https://docs.rs/pool/struct.McpConnectionPool.html)>

Direct access to the underlying pool, in case the embedder wants to inspect or mutate it directly.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lash_plugin_mcp/plugin.rs.html#56-62)#### pub async fn [attach_server](https://docs.rs#method.attach_server)(
    &self,
    server_name: [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html),
    config: [McpServerConfig](https://docs.rs/config/enum.McpServerConfig.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [McpError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.McpError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lash_plugin_mcp/plugin.rs.html#56-62)

#### pub async fn [attach_server](https://docs.rs#method.attach_server)(
    &self,
    server_name: [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html),
    config: [McpServerConfig](https://docs.rs/config/enum.McpServerConfig.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [McpError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.McpError.html)>

Attach a new server at runtime. The new tools become visible to any session created after this call returns; existing sessions will see the new tools after their next tool-catalog refresh.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lash_plugin_mcp/pool.rs.html#105-123)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lash_plugin_mcp/pool.rs.html#105-123)

Build a pool for the configured servers. Each server is tried eagerly in turn so tools are available immediately when servers are up, but a connection failure never aborts construction: the entry stays registered and reconnects in the background. Only configuration errors (a misconfigured server, not an outage) fail the build.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lash_plugin_mcp/pool.rs.html#128-138)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lash_plugin_mcp/pool.rs.html#128-138)

Add (or replace) one server in the pool. Connects eagerly and returns the definitive result — use this for interactive attach, where the caller wants to know whether the server is reachable.

Remove and shut down one server.

# lash_plugin_mcp::naming - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lash-plugin-mcp/0.1.0-alpha.82/lash_plugin_mcp/naming/index.html

## Expand description

Tool name prefixing helpers. Moved verbatim from `crates/lash/src/mcp.rs` so the
`mcp__<server>__<tool>` naming scheme keeps producing identical names
(avoids breaking config files / saved trajectories that reference tools
by their full prefixed name).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_prefixed_name.html)- prefixed_ - name
- Build the prefixed tool name (`mcp__<server>__<tool>`) and discovery metadata for one MCP tool. The original (unnormalised) tool name is kept as an alias so users can search/find by the server’s native name.
- [normalize_](https://docs.rs/fn.normalize_identifier.html)- identifier
- Normalise a server name or raw MCP tool name to lowercase ASCII
alphanumeric and underscore. Collapses runs of non-alphanumeric characters
into a single `_`, trims trailing underscores, and falls back to`"tool"`if the input has no usable characters.
- [unique_](https://docs.rs/fn.unique_prefixed_name.html)- prefixed_ - name
- Ensure `base`is unique against`used_names`. Appends`_2`,`_3`, … until a free name is found. The returned name is also recorded in`used_names`.

# lash_plugin_mcp::pool - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lash-plugin-mcp/0.1.0-alpha.82/lash_plugin_mcp/pool/index.html

## Expand description

Per-core MCP connection pool.

[ McpConnectionPool](https://docs.rs/struct.McpConnectionPool.html) holds one client per configured server and is shared
across every session built from the same [

`lash_core::LashCore`]. The pool
attempts to connect each server eagerly when constructed, but a server
that is down never fails construction: the entry stays registered and a
background task retries with exponential backoff until it connects (or the
server is detached). A connection that dies mid-life is detected on the
next tool call and re-established the same way. Imported tool definitions
are kept across a disconnect so the tool catalog stays stable; calls to a
disconnected server fail loudly instead.The wire-level transport is provided by the official [ rmcp](https://docs.rs/rmcp/1.6.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rmcp/index.html) SDK.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [McpConnection](https://docs.rs/struct.McpConnectionPool.html)- Pool
- Shared, per-core connection pool. Wrapped in `Arc`and cloned into each session plugin instance.
- [McpServer](https://docs.rs/struct.McpServerStatus.html)- Status
- Connection status of one configured server, for host/UI observability.

---

# lash-llm-tools 0.1.0-alpha.82 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lash-llm-tools/0.1.0-alpha.82

# lash

A Rust runtime for durable LLM agents.

Most agent stacks treat the LLM as the runtime and stitch state around it — a database for memory, a queue for retries, a sandbox for code. `lash` inverts that. The runtime is the durable end of the pair; the LLM is the variable call. Your app owns the outer boundaries — storage, auth, transport, product state. `lash` owns the turn — model calls, modes, tools, plugins, semantic stream events, usage, and terminal outcomes.

**Docs:** [https://lash.run/](https://lash.run/) — quickstart, embedding guide, tools, plugins, persistence, durable-workflow integration, and architecture chapters.

Alpha:works today, API still moving fast — pin to an exact`=0.1.0-alpha.N`version when you embed.

## What's inside

- **Durable per-turn commits**— every completed turn lands as one atomic- `RuntimeCommit`against a- `SessionGraph`. Effects are the replay boundary; turns are the semantic commit boundary. →- [persistence](https://lash.run/persistence.html)
- **Workflow-host integration**— a sans-IO turn machine behind one- `EffectHost`boundary. The default- `InlineEffectHost`runs in-process; the first-party Restate adapter replays effects from host history, exposes invocation identity for host cancellation and inspection, and retries the final idempotent commit. →- [durability](https://lash.run/architecture/durability.html)
- **Two execution modes, one commit unit**—- `standard`uses native provider tool-calling with concurrent dispatch;- `rlm`runs- `lashlang`programs in a sandboxed VM where every effect crosses the host. →- [RLM](https://lash.run/rlm.html)
- **Tool providers and plugins**— ordinary host operations are- `ToolProvider`s; plugins add runtime/session behavior such as prompts, planning, memory, subagents, history transforms, UI activity, catalog policy, and tool-output budgeting. Hosts compose only what they embed. →- [tools](https://lash.run/tools.html),- [plugins](https://lash.run/plugins.html)
- **Provider portability**— Anthropic, OpenAI Responses, any OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions endpoint, OpenAI Codex, and Google Gemini / Code Assist. MCP servers attach through- `lash-plugin-mcp`. →- [providers](https://lash.run/architecture/providers.html)
- **Tracing as a first-class sink**— attach a- `TraceSink`for structured turn, tool, LLM, prompt, and usage records. Bundled JSONL sink + self-contained HTML viewer; optional OpenTelemetry export. →- [tracing](https://lash.run/tracing.html)

## Embed it

`lash` ships on crates.io as `lash-runtime` (the bare name is taken), but is still imported as `lash`. During the alpha the dep needs the explicit pre-release tag:

```
[]
         = "=0.1.0-alpha.82"
 = "=0.1.0-alpha.82"
               = "1"
                = {  = "1",  = ["full"] }
```
```
use Arc;
use ;
use ;
async
```
Full walkthrough in the [quickstart](https://lash.run/quickstart.html); the complete facade API — session specs, plugin stacks, turn streaming, persistence, subagents, MCP, durable workflows — is in the [embedding guide](https://lash.run/embedding.html). To wrap Lash behind a service boundary (HTTP, queues, workflow handlers), use the canonical DTOs from `lash::remote` — see [remote protocol](https://lash.run/remote-protocol.html).

## Examples

Two runnable apps under `examples/` drive the facade end-to-end: full hosts with
a browser UI, real persistence, remote DTO streams, and optional durable
execution. Start with `agent-service` for the smallest production-shaped browser
embedding: app-owned product state, a Lash session per chat, and session
observation live replay for reconnect. Move to `agent-workbench` when you want
the advanced Restate host with durable processes, triggers, cron, and the same
cursor-based browser stream. The docs walk through both at
[https://lash.run/examples.html](https://lash.run/examples.html).

```
# SQLite-backed chat app: RLM, app-owned tools, streaming, optional Restate turns
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...
# Adds durable background work: Lashlang processes, subagents, cron triggers (Restate required)
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...
```
See each example's README for environment knobs and Restate recipes.

## The CLI

`lash-cli` is a first-party terminal frontend on top of the library — patch-based editing, shell execution, file/web search, planning, subagents, session resume, live token accounting. Not the product, but a fully featured way to drive the runtime and a useful end-to-end reference.

```
 |
# or: cargo build -p lash-cli --release
```
CLI reference: [https://lash.run/cli.html](https://lash.run/cli.html).

## Contributing

Feature requests and bug reports welcome — open an [issue](https://github.com/SamGalanakis/lash/issues). At this alpha stage detailed write-ups (what you tried, expected, and saw) help more than drive-by PRs — see [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://docs.rs/CONTRIBUTING.md).

# jsonschema - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jsonschema/^0.18/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#jsonschema)jsonschema

A crate for performing fast JSON Schema validation. It is fast due to schema compilation into a validation tree, which reduces runtime costs for working with schema parameters.

Supports:

- JSON Schema drafts 4, 6, 7 (except some optional test cases);
- Loading remote documents via HTTP(S);

Partially supported drafts (some keywords are not implemented):

- Draft 2019-09 (requires the `draft201909`feature enabled)
- Draft 2020-12 (requires the `draft202012`feature enabled)

This library is functional and ready for use, but its API is still evolving to the 1.0 API.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage-examples)Usage Examples:

A schema can be compiled with two main flavours:

- using default configurations

`let compiled_schema = JSONSchema::compile(&schema).expect("A valid schema");`- using custom configurations (such as define a Draft version)

```
let compiled_schema = JSONSchema::options()
    .with_draft(Draft::Draft7)
    .compile(&schema)
    .expect("A valid schema");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-cli-tool-to-highlight-print-errors)Example (CLI tool to highlight print errors)

```
use jsonschema::{Draft, JSONSchema};
use serde_json::json;
let schema = json!({"maxLength": 5});
let instance = json!("foo");
let compiled = JSONSchema::options()
    .with_draft(Draft::Draft7)
    .compile(&schema)
    .expect("A valid schema");
let result = compiled.validate(&instance);
if let Err(errors) = result {
    for error in errors {
        println!("Validation error: {}", error);
        println!("Instance path: {}", error.instance_path);
    }
}
```
Each error has an `instance_path` attribute that indicates the path to the erroneous part within the validated instance.
It could be transformed to JSON Pointer via `.to_string()` or to `Vec<String>` via `.into_vec()`.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- Error types
- Facilities for working with paths within schemas or validated instances.
- Primitive types for property type validators

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- Full configuration to guide the`JSONSchema`compilation.
- The structure that holds a JSON Schema compiled into a validation tree

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- JSON Schema Draft version

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- Trait that allows implementing custom validation for keywords.
- A resolver that resolves external schema references. Internal references such as`#/definitions`and JSON pointers are handled internally.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- A shortcut for validating`instance`against`schema`. Draft version is detected automatically.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- An opaque error type that is returned by resolvers on resolution failures.

[75](#75)impl LlmToolsProvider {
[76](#76)    async fn llm_query(&self, args: &Value, context: &ToolContext<'_>) -> Result<Value, String> {
[77](#77)        let task = required_string(args, "task")?;
[78](#78)        let inputs = args.get("inputs").cloned().unwrap_or(Value::Null);
[79](#79)        let output_schema = lash_lashlang_runtime::parse_output_schema(args.get("output"))?;
[80](#80)        let session_model = context
[81](#81)            .sessions()
[82](#82)            .model()
[83](#83)            .await
[84](#84)            .map_err(|err| format!("failed to read current session model: {err}"))?;
[85](#85)        let model = self.model.clone().unwrap_or(session_model.model);
[86](#86)        let model_variant = self.model_variant.clone().or(session_model.model_variant);
[87](#87)        let response_schema = llm_query_response_schema(output_schema.as_ref());
[88](#88)        let prompt = llm_query_prompt(&task, &inputs, output_schema.as_ref());
[89](#89)
[90](#90)        let output = DirectOutputSpec::JsonSchema(DirectJsonSchema {
[91](#91)            name: "llm_query_result".to_string(),
[92](#92)            schema: response_schema.clone().into(),
[93](#93)            strict: true,
[94](#94)        });
[95](#95)
[96](#96)        let completion = context
[97](#97)            .direct_completions()
[98](#98)            .complete(
[99](#99)                DirectRequest {
[100](#100)                    model,
[101](#101)                    model_variant,
[102](#102)                    messages: vec![
[103](#103)                        DirectMessage {
[104](#104)                            role: DirectRole::System,
[105](#105)                            parts: vec![DirectPart::Text(
[106](#106)                                "Answer the focused sub-question using only the supplied task and inputs. Return only JSON matching the requested result wrapper. Use kind=\"error\" with a concise error only when the task cannot be answered from the supplied inputs."
[107](#107)                                    .to_string(),
[108](#108)                            )],
[109](#109)                        },
[110](#110)                        DirectMessage {
[111](#111)                            role: DirectRole::User,
[112](#112)                            parts: vec![DirectPart::Text(prompt)],
[113](#113)                        },
[114](#114)                    ],
[115](#115)                    attachments: Vec::new(),
[116](#116)                    output,
[117](#117)                    stream_events: None,
[118](#118)                    generation: lash_core::GenerationOptions::default(),
[119](#119)                    session_id: Some(format!("{}-llm-query", context.session_id())),
[120](#120)                    caused_by: None,
[121](#121)                    replay: None,
[122](#122)                },
[123](#123)                "llm_query",
[124](#124)            )
[125](#125)            .await
[126](#126)            .map_err(|err| format!("llm_query failed: {err}"))?;
[127](#127)
[128](#128)        parse_llm_query_result(&completion.text, &response_schema)
[129](#129)    }

[143](#143)pub fn llm_query_tool_definition() -> ToolDefinition {
[144](#144)    tool_definition(
[145](#145)        "llm_query",
[146](#146)        "Run a one-shot LLM prompt over supplied data and return its result. The `task` plus everything in `inputs` is rendered into that single prompt; the call cannot use tools, inspect files, or gather more context beyond what you pass it. Use this for extracting information, classification, summarization, judging, or transformation over data already in your variables. `inputs` can be any structured value. `output` is optional and defaults to a string; when present, it requests structured output using record descriptors or `Type { ... }` literals.",
[147](#147)        llm_query_input_schema(),
[148](#148)        vec![
[149](#149)            r#"summary = await llm.query({ task: "Summarize the supplied notes in three bullets", inputs: { notes: notes } })?"#.into(),
[150](#150)            r#"claims = await llm.query({ task: "Extract the key claim from each supplied chunk", inputs: { chunks: chunks }, output: { claims: "list[str]" } })?"#.into(),
[151](#151)        ],
[152](#152)        ToolScheduling::Parallel,
[153](#153)    )
[154](#154)    .with_lashlang_binding(LashlangToolBinding::new(["llm"], "query"))
[155](#155)    .with_output_from_input_schema("output", Some(json!({ "type": "string" })))
[156](#156)}
[157](#157)
[158](#158)fn llm_query_input_schema() -> Value {
[159](#159)    json!({
[160](#160)        "type": "object",
[161](#161)        "properties": {
[162](#162)            "task": { "type": "string" },
[163](#163)            "inputs": {},
[164](#164)            "output": { "type": "object", "additionalProperties": true }
[165](#165)        },
[166](#166)        "required": ["task"],
[167](#167)        "additionalProperties": false
[168](#168)    })
[169](#169)}
[170](#170)
[171](#171)fn llm_query_prompt(task: &str, inputs: &Value, output_schema: Option<&Value>) -> String {
[172](#172)    let mut sections = Vec::new();
[173](#173)    sections.push(format!("Task:\n{task}"));
[174](#174)    sections.push(format!(
[175](#175)        "Inputs:\n```json\n{}\n```",
[176](#176)        serde_json::to_string_pretty(inputs).unwrap_or_else(|_| inputs.to_string())
[177](#177)    ));
[178](#178)    if let Some(schema) = output_schema {
[179](#179)        sections.push(format!(
[180](#180)            "Return `kind=\"value\"` with `value` matching this JSON Schema, or `kind=\"error\"` with a concise error if the task cannot be answered from the supplied inputs:\n```json\n{}\n```",
[181](#181)            serde_json::to_string_pretty(schema).unwrap_or_else(|_| schema.to_string())
[182](#182)        ));
[183](#183)    } else {
[184](#184)        sections.push("Return `kind=\"value\"` with a concise string `value`, or `kind=\"error\"` with a concise error if the task cannot be answered from the supplied inputs.".to_string());
[185](#185)    }
[186](#186)    sections.join("\n\n")
[187](#187)}
[188](#188)
[189](#189)fn llm_query_response_schema(output_schema: Option<&Value>) -> Value {
[190](#190)    let value_schema = output_schema
[191](#191)        .cloned()
[192](#192)        .unwrap_or_else(|| json!({"type": "string"}));
[193](#193)    json!({
[194](#194)        "type": "object",
[195](#195)        "additionalProperties": false,
[196](#196)        "required": ["kind", "value", "error"],
[197](#197)        "properties": {
[198](#198)            "kind": { "type": "string", "enum": ["value", "error"] },
[199](#199)            "value": {
[200](#200)                "anyOf": [
[201](#201)                    value_schema,
[202](#202)                    { "type": "null" }
[203](#203)                ]
[204](#204)            },
[205](#205)            "error": {
[206](#206)                "anyOf": [
[207](#207)                    { "type": "string" },
[208](#208)                    { "type": "null" }
[209](#209)                ]
[210](#210)            }
[211](#211)        }
[212](#212)    })
[213](#213)}
[214](#214)
[215](#215)fn parse_llm_query_result(text: &str, schema: &Value) -> Result<Value, String> {
[216](#216)    let trimmed = text.trim();
[217](#217)    if trimmed.is_empty() {
[218](#218)        return Err("llm_query returned empty output".to_string());
[219](#219)    }
[220](#220)    let value = serde_json::from_str::<Value>(trimmed).or_else(|err| {
[221](#221)        let Some(start) = trimmed.find(['{', '[', '"']) else {
[222](#222)            return Err(format!("llm_query returned non-JSON output: {err}"));
[223](#223)        };
[224](#224)        let end = trimmed
[225](#225)            .rfind(['}', ']', '"'])
[226](#226)            .ok_or_else(|| format!("llm_query returned malformed JSON output: {err}"))?;
[227](#227)        if end < start {
[228](#228)            return Err(format!("llm_query returned malformed JSON output: {err}"));
[229](#229)        }
[230](#230)        serde_json::from_str::<Value>(&trimmed[start..=end])
[231](#231)            .map_err(|parse_err| format!("llm_query returned malformed JSON output: {parse_err}"))
[232](#232)    })?;
[233](#233)    let compiled = jsonschema::JSONSchema::compile(schema)
[234](#234)        .map_err(|err| format!("llm_query output schema is invalid: {err}"))?;
[235](#235)    if let Err(errors) = compiled.validate(&value) {
[236](#236)        let message = errors
[237](#237)            .map(|err| err.to_string())
[238](#238)            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
[239](#239)            .join("; ");
[240](#240)        return Err(format!("llm_query output did not match schema: {message}"));
[241](#241)    }
[242](#242)    match value.get("kind").and_then(Value::as_str) {
[243](#243)        Some("value") => value
[244](#244)            .get("value")
[245](#245)            .cloned()
[246](#246)            .filter(|value| !value.is_null())
[247](#247)            .ok_or_else(|| "llm_query returned value result without value".to_string()),
[248](#248)        Some("error") => Err(value
[249](#249)            .get("error")
[250](#250)            .and_then(Value::as_str)
[251](#251)            .map(str::trim)
[252](#252)            .filter(|message| !message.is_empty())
[253](#253)            .unwrap_or("llm_query returned an error")
[254](#254)            .to_string()),
[255](#255)        Some(other) => Err(format!("llm_query returned unknown result kind `{other}`")),
[256](#256)        None => Err("llm_query returned result without kind field".to_string()),
[257](#257)    }
[258](#258)}
[259](#259)
[260](#260)fn tool_definition(
[261](#261)    name: &str,
[262](#262)    description: impl Into<String>,
[263](#263)    input_schema: Value,
[264](#264)    examples: Vec<String>,
[265](#265)    execution_mode: ToolScheduling,
[266](#266)) -> ToolDefinition {
[267](#267)    ToolDefinition::raw(
[268](#268)        format!("tool:{name}"),
[269](#269)        name,
[270](#270)        description,
[271](#271)        input_schema,
[272](#272)        json!({ "type": "object", "additionalProperties": true }),
[273](#273)    )
[274](#274)    .with_examples(examples)
[275](#275)    .with_scheduling(execution_mode)
[276](#276)}
[277](#277)
[278](#278)fn required_string(args: &Value, key: &str) -> Result<String, String> {
[279](#279)    args.get(key)
[280](#280)        .and_then(Value::as_str)
[281](#281)        .map(str::trim)
[282](#282)        .filter(|value| !value.is_empty())
[283](#283)        .map(ToOwned::to_owned)
[284](#284)        .ok_or_else(|| format!("missing required parameter: {key}"))
[285](#285)}
[286](#286)
[287](#287)fn finalise_tool_result(result: Result<Value, String>) -> ToolResult {
[288](#288)    match result {
[289](#289)        Ok(value) => ToolResult::ok(value),
[290](#290)        Err(err) => ToolResult::err(json!(err)),
[291](#291)    }
[292](#292)}

[376](#376)    #[test]
[377](#377)    fn llm_definitions_include_llm_query_only() {

# yatrosci-special 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/yatrosci-special/0.1.0

Special mathematical functions for scientific computing,
providing functionality equivalent to `scipy.special`.

## Overview

This crate provides:

- Gamma and related functions (gamma, lgamma, digamma, beta)
- Bessel functions (J, Y, I, K)
- Error functions (erf, erfc, erfinv)
- Airy functions
- Elliptic functions and integrals
- Hypergeometric functions
- Orthogonal polynomials (Legendre, Hermite, Laguerre, Chebyshev)
- Spherical harmonics
- Zeta and related functions

## Example

```
use ;
// Gamma function
let g = gamma;  // = 4! = 24
// Error function
let e = erf;  // ≈ 0.8427
// Bessel function
let j0 = bessel_j0;  // ≈ 0.7652
```

---

                    yatrosci-special 0.1.0

                Special mathematical functions for SciRS - Bessel, Gamma, erf, etc.

# thiserror - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/thiserror/^2.0/

## Expand description

This library provides a convenient derive macro for the standard library’s
[ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/error/trait.Error.html) trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use thiserror::Error;
#[derive(Error, Debug)]
pub enum DataStoreError {
    #[error("data store disconnected")]
    Disconnect(#[from] io::Error),
    #[error("the data for key `{0}` is not available")]
    Redaction(String),
    #[error("invalid header (expected {expected:?}, found {found:?})")]
    InvalidHeader {
        expected: String,
        found: String,
    },
    #[error("unknown data store error")]
    Unknown,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

-
Thiserror deliberately does not appear in your public API. You get the same thing as if you had written an implementation of `std::error::Error`
-
Errors may be enums, structs with named fields, tuple structs, or unit structs.
-
A `Display``#[error("...")]`messages on the struct or each variant of your enum, as shown above in the example.The messages support a shorthand for interpolating fields from the error. - `#[error("{var}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.0)`
- `#[error("{var:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.0)`
 These shorthands can be used together with any additional format args, which may be arbitrary expressions. For example: `#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("invalid rdo_lookahead_frames {0} (expected < {max})", max = i32::MAX)] InvalidLookahead(u32), }`If one of the additional expression arguments needs to refer to a field of the struct or enum, then refer to named fields as `.var`and tuple fields as`.0`.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("first letter must be lowercase but was {:?}", first_char(.0))] WrongCase(String), #[error("invalid index {idx}, expected at least {} and at most {}", .limits.lo, .limits.hi)] OutOfBounds { idx: usize, limits: Limits }, }`
-
A `From``#[from]`attribute.The variant using `#[from]`must not contain any other fields beyond the source error (and possibly a backtrace — see below). Usually`#[from]`fields are unnamed, but`#[from]`is allowed on a named field too.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io(#[from] io::Error), Glob(#[from] globset::Error), }`
-
The Error trait’s `source()``#[source]`attribute or is named`source`, if any. This is for identifying the underlying lower level error that caused your error.The `#[from]`attribute always implies that the same field is`#[source]`, so you don’t ever need to specify both attributes.Any error type that implements `std::error::Error`or dereferences to`dyn std::error::Error`will work as a source.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, #[source] // optional if field name is `source` source: anyhow::Error, }`
-
The Error trait’s `provide()``Backtrace`, if any, as a`std::backtrace::Backtrace``Backtrace`in errors requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`use std::backtrace::Backtrace; #[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, backtrace: Backtrace, // automatically detected }`
-
If a field is both a source (named `source`, or has`#[source]`or`#[from]`attribute)*and*is marked`#[backtrace]`, then the Error trait’s`provide()``provide`so that both layers of the error share the same backtrace. The`#[backtrace]`attribute requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[backtrace] source: io::Error, }, }`
-
For variants that use `#[from]`and also contain a`Backtrace`field, a backtrace is captured from within the`From`impl.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[from] source: io::Error, backtrace: Backtrace, }, }`
-
Errors may use `error(transparent)`to forward the source and`Display``#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { ... #[error(transparent)] Other(#[from] anyhow::Error), // source and Display delegate to anyhow::Error }`Another use case is hiding implementation details of an error representation behind an opaque error type, so that the representation is able to evolve without breaking the crate’s public API. `// PublicError is public, but opaque and easy to keep compatible. #[derive(Error, Debug)] #[error(transparent)] pub struct PublicError(#[from] ErrorRepr); impl PublicError { // Accessors for anything we do want to expose publicly. } // Private and free to change across minor version of the crate. #[derive(Error, Debug)] enum ErrorRepr { ... }`
-
See also the `anyhow`

---

# yatrosci_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-core/^0.1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#scirs-core)SciRS Core

Core traits, types, and error handling for the SciRS scientific computing ecosystem.

This crate provides the foundational abstractions used throughout SciRS:

- `Scalar`trait for numeric types
- `Float`trait for floating-point operations
- Complex number utilities
- Error types and result aliases
- Precision control

[§](https://docs.rs#canonical-references)Canonical References

The `Float` and `Scalar` traits expose IEEE 754-2019 standard operations
(epsilon, infinity, NaN, fused multiply-add) with no deviation from the standard.
All implementations delegate to the `num-traits` crate which in turn delegates
to the Rust standard library’s IEEE 754-compliant primitives.

- IEEE (2019). *IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic*(IEEE 754-2019). DOI:[10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229](https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229)
- Higham, N.J. (2002). *Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms*(2nd ed.), §2.2 (Floating-point arithmetic model), pp. 36–50. SIAM. DOI:[10.1137/1.9780898718027](https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898718027)

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use yatrosci_core::{Scalar, Float, Complex64};
fn compute<T: Float>(x: T) -> T {
    x.sin() + x.cos()
}
```

# approx - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/approx/^0.5/

## Expand description

A crate that provides facilities for testing the approximate equality of floating-point based types, using either relative difference, or units in the last place (ULPs) comparisons.

You can also use the `*_{eq, ne}!` and `assert_*_{eq, ne}!` macros to test for equality using a
more positional style:

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate approx;
use std::f64;
abs_diff_eq!(1.0, 1.0);
abs_diff_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0, max_relative = 1.0);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON, max_relative = 1.0);
relative_eq!(1.0, 1.0, max_relative = 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0, max_ulps = 4);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0, epsilon = f64::EPSILON, max_ulps = 4);
ulps_eq!(1.0, 1.0, max_ulps = 4, epsilon = f64::EPSILON);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-approximate-equality-for-custom-types)Implementing approximate equality for custom types

The `*Eq` traits allow approximate equalities to be implemented on types, based on the
fundamental floating point implementations.

For example, we might want to be able to do approximate assertions on a complex number type:

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate approx;
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Complex<T> {
    x: T,
    i: T,
}
let x = Complex { x: 1.2, i: 2.3 };
assert_relative_eq!(x, x);
assert_ulps_eq!(x, x, max_ulps = 4);
```
To do this we can implement [ AbsDiffEq](https://docs.rs/trait.AbsDiffEq.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/trait.RelativeEq.html)

`RelativeEq`[generically in terms of a type parameter that also implements](https://docs.rs/trait.UlpsEq.html)

`UlpsEq``AbsDiffEq`, `RelativeEq` and `UlpsEq` respectively.
This means that we can make comparisons for either `Complex<f32>` or `Complex<f64>`:```
impl<T: AbsDiffEq> AbsDiffEq for Complex<T> where
    T::Epsilon: Copy,
{
    type Epsilon = T::Epsilon;
    fn default_epsilon() -> T::Epsilon {
        T::default_epsilon()
    }
    fn abs_diff_eq(&self, other: &Self, epsilon: T::Epsilon) -> bool {
        T::abs_diff_eq(&self.x, &other.x, epsilon) &&
        T::abs_diff_eq(&self.i, &other.i, epsilon)
    }
}
impl<T: RelativeEq> RelativeEq for Complex<T> where
    T::Epsilon: Copy,
{
    fn default_max_relative() -> T::Epsilon {
        T::default_max_relative()
    }
    fn relative_eq(&self, other: &Self, epsilon: T::Epsilon, max_relative: T::Epsilon) -> bool {
        T::relative_eq(&self.x, &other.x, epsilon, max_relative) &&
        T::relative_eq(&self.i, &other.i, epsilon, max_relative)
    }
}
impl<T: UlpsEq> UlpsEq for Complex<T> where
    T::Epsilon: Copy,
{
    fn default_max_ulps() -> u32 {
        T::default_max_ulps()
    }
    fn ulps_eq(&self, other: &Self, epsilon: T::Epsilon, max_ulps: u32) -> bool {
        T::ulps_eq(&self.x, &other.x, epsilon, max_ulps) &&
        T::ulps_eq(&self.i, &other.i, epsilon, max_ulps)
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#references)References

Floating point is hard! Thanks goes to these links for helping to make things a *little*
easier to understand:

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [abs_](https://docs.rs/macro.abs_diff_eq.html)- diff_ - eq
- Approximate equality of using the absolute difference.
- [abs_](https://docs.rs/macro.abs_diff_ne.html)- diff_ - ne
- Approximate inequality of using the absolute difference.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_abs_diff_eq.html)- abs_ - diff_ - eq
- An assertion that delegates to `abs_diff_eq!`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_abs_diff_ne.html)- abs_ - diff_ - ne
- An assertion that delegates to `abs_diff_ne!`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_relative_eq.html)- relative_ - eq
- An assertion that delegates to `relative_eq!`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_relative_ne.html)- relative_ - ne
- An assertion that delegates to `relative_ne!`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_ulps_eq.html)- ulps_ - eq
- An assertion that delegates to `ulps_eq!`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_ulps_ne.html)- ulps_ - ne
- An assertion that delegates to `ulps_ne!`
- [relative_](https://docs.rs/macro.relative_eq.html)- eq
- Approximate equality using both the absolute difference and relative based comparisons.
- [relative_](https://docs.rs/macro.relative_ne.html)- ne
- Approximate inequality using both the absolute difference and relative based comparisons.
- [ulps_eq](https://docs.rs/macro.ulps_eq.html)
- Approximate equality using both the absolute difference and ULPs (Units in Last Place).
- [ulps_ne](https://docs.rs/macro.ulps_ne.html)
- Approximate inequality using both the absolute difference and ULPs (Units in Last Place).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AbsDiff](https://docs.rs/struct.AbsDiff.html)
- The requisite parameters for testing for approximate equality using a absolute difference based comparison.
- [Relative](https://docs.rs/struct.Relative.html)
- The requisite parameters for testing for approximate equality using a relative based comparison.
- [Ulps](https://docs.rs/struct.Ulps.html)
- The requisite parameters for testing for approximate equality using an ULPs based comparison.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AbsDiff](https://docs.rs/trait.AbsDiffEq.html)- Eq
- Equality that is defined using the absolute difference of two numbers.
- [Relative](https://docs.rs/trait.RelativeEq.html)- Eq
- Equality comparisons between two numbers using both the absolute difference and relative based comparisons.
- [UlpsEq](https://docs.rs/trait.UlpsEq.html)
- Equality comparisons between two numbers using both the absolute difference and ULPs (Units in Last Place) based comparisons.

# yatrosci_special - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/target-redirect/yatrosci_special/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#scirs-special-functions)SciRS Special Functions

Special mathematical functions for scientific computing,
providing functionality equivalent to `scipy.special`.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

This crate provides:

- Gamma and related functions (gamma, lgamma, digamma, beta)
- Bessel functions (J, Y, I, K)
- Error functions (erf, erfc, erfinv)
- Airy functions
- Elliptic functions and integrals
- Hypergeometric functions
- Orthogonal polynomials (Legendre, Hermite, Laguerre, Chebyshev)
- Spherical harmonics
- Zeta and related functions

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use yatrosci_special::{gamma, erf, bessel_j0, legendre_p};
// Gamma function
let g = gamma(5.0);  // = 4! = 24
// Error function
let e = erf(1.0);  // ≈ 0.8427
// Bessel function
let j0 = bessel_j0(1.0);  // ≈ 0.7652
```

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- Elliptic integrals and functions

- Error function and related functions

- Gamma function module

- Hypergeometric functions ₁F₁, ₂F₁.
