[2749](https://docs.rs#2749)
[2750](https://docs.rs#2750)#[cfg(test)]
[2751](https://docs.rs#2751)mod tests {
[2752](https://docs.rs#2752)    use super::*;
[2753](https://docs.rs#2753)
[2754](https://docs.rs#2754)    #[test]
[2755](https://docs.rs#2755)    fn test_gamma() {
[2756](https://docs.rs#2756)        // Gamma(5) = 4! = 24
[2757](https://docs.rs#2757)        assert!((gamma(5.0) - 24.0).abs() < 1e-10);
[2758](https://docs.rs#2758)
[2759](https://docs.rs#2759)        // Gamma(0.5) = sqrt(pi)
[2760](https://docs.rs#2760)        assert!((gamma(0.5) - std::f64::consts::PI.sqrt()).abs() < 1e-10);
[2761](https://docs.rs#2761)    }
[2762](https://docs.rs#2762)
[2763](https://docs.rs#2763)    #[test]
[2764](https://docs.rs#2764)    fn sph_harm_real_known_exact_values() {
[2765](https://docs.rs#2765)        use std::f64::consts::PI;
[2766](https://docs.rs#2766)        // Y_0^0 = 1/(2√π) for all angles (exact).
[2767](https://docs.rs#2767)        assert!((sph_harm_real(0, 0, 1.1, 2.3) - 0.5 / PI.sqrt()).abs() < 1e-12);
[2768](https://docs.rs#2768)        // Y_1^0 at the north pole (θ=0) = √(3/4π).
[2769](https://docs.rs#2769)        let y10 = sph_harm_real(1, 0, 0.0, 0.0);
[2770](https://docs.rs#2770)        assert!((y10 - (3.0 / (4.0 * PI)).sqrt()).abs() < 1e-12, "Y_1^0 = {y10}");
[2771](https://docs.rs#2771)        // Y_1^{+1} at θ=π/2, φ=0 = √(3/4π)  (the real p_x orbital, POSITIVE).
[2772](https://docs.rs#2772)        let y11 = sph_harm_real(1, 1, PI / 2.0, 0.0);
[2773](https://docs.rs#2773)        assert!((y11 - (3.0 / (4.0 * PI)).sqrt()).abs() < 1e-12, "Y_1^1 = {y11}");
[2774](https://docs.rs#2774)        // m out of range → 0.
[2775](https://docs.rs#2775)        assert_eq!(sph_harm_real(1, 2, 0.5, 0.5), 0.0);
[2776](https://docs.rs#2776)    }
[2777](https://docs.rs#2777)
[2778](https://docs.rs#2778)    #[test]
[2779](https://docs.rs#2779)    fn sph_harm_real_is_orthonormal() {
[2780](https://docs.rs#2780)        use std::f64::consts::PI;
[2781](https://docs.rs#2781)        // INVARIANT: ∫|Y_l^m|² dΩ = 1. Numerically integrate Y_2^1 over the
[2782](https://docs.rs#2782)        // sphere (independent of the closed-form normalization constant).
[2783](https://docs.rs#2783)        let (nt, np) = (400usize, 400usize);
[2784](https://docs.rs#2784)        let mut integral = 0.0;
[2785](https://docs.rs#2785)        for i in 0..nt {
[2786](https://docs.rs#2786)            let theta = (i as f64 + 0.5) / nt as f64 * PI;
[2787](https://docs.rs#2787)            let dt = PI / nt as f64;
[2788](https://docs.rs#2788)            for j in 0..np {
[2789](https://docs.rs#2789)                let phi = (j as f64 + 0.5) / np as f64 * 2.0 * PI;
[2790](https://docs.rs#2790)                let dp = 2.0 * PI / np as f64;
[2791](https://docs.rs#2791)                let y = sph_harm_real(2, 1, theta, phi);
[2792](https://docs.rs#2792)                integral += y * y * theta.sin() * dt * dp;
[2793](https://docs.rs#2793)            }
[2794](https://docs.rs#2794)        }
[2795](https://docs.rs#2795)        assert!((integral - 1.0).abs() < 1e-3, "∫|Y_2^1|² dΩ = {integral}");
[2796](https://docs.rs#2796)    }
[2797](https://docs.rs#2797)
[2798](https://docs.rs#2798)    // ── lambertw ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[2799](https://docs.rs#2799)
[2800](https://docs.rs#2800)    #[test]
[2801](https://docs.rs#2801)    fn lambertw_invariant_w_exp_w_eq_z() {
[2802](https://docs.rs#2802)        // Primary invariant: W(z)·eᵂ⁽ᶻ⁾ = z (DLMF 4.13.1)
[2803](https://docs.rs#2803)        for &z in &[0.1_f64, 1.0, std::f64::consts::E, 10.0, 100.0] {
[2804](https://docs.rs#2804)            let w = lambertw(z).unwrap();
[2805](https://docs.rs#2805)            let residual = w * w.exp() - z;
[2806](https://docs.rs#2806)            assert!(residual.abs() < 1e-12 * z, "W({z})·eᵂ−z = {residual}");
[2807](https://docs.rs#2807)        }
[2808](https://docs.rs#2808)    }
[2809](https://docs.rs#2809)
[2810](https://docs.rs#2810)    #[test]
[2811](https://docs.rs#2811)    fn lambertw_known_values() {
[2812](https://docs.rs#2812)        // W(1) = Omega constant ≈ 0.5671432904 (scipy 1.13 fixture)
[2813](https://docs.rs#2813)        assert!((lambertw(1.0).unwrap() - 0.567_143_290_409_784).abs() < 1e-12);
[2814](https://docs.rs#2814)        // W(e) = 1 exactly (closed form: e·e^1 = e·e = e²? No: W(e)·eᵂ=e → W=1 → 1·e=e ✓)
[2815](https://docs.rs#2815)        assert!((lambertw(std::f64::consts::E).unwrap() - 1.0).abs() < 1e-13);
[2816](https://docs.rs#2816)        // W(10) (scipy fixture)
[2817](https://docs.rs#2817)        assert!((lambertw(10.0).unwrap() - 1.745_528_002_740_7).abs() < 1e-10);
[2818](https://docs.rs#2818)        // W(100) (scipy fixture)
[2819](https://docs.rs#2819)        assert!((lambertw(100.0).unwrap() - 3.385_630_140_290_05).abs() < 1e-11);
[2820](https://docs.rs#2820)        // W(0) = 0 (trivial)
[2821](https://docs.rs#2821)        assert_eq!(lambertw(0.0).unwrap(), 0.0);
[2822](https://docs.rs#2822)    }
[2823](https://docs.rs#2823)

[2830](https://docs.rs#2830)    // ── zeta ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[2831](https://docs.rs#2831)
[2832](https://docs.rs#2832)    #[test]
[2833](https://docs.rs#2833)    fn zeta_basel_and_exact_values() {
[2834](https://docs.rs#2834)        use std::f64::consts::PI;
[2835](https://docs.rs#2835)        // ζ(2) = π²/6 (Basel problem, Euler 1735; DLMF 25.6.2)
[2836](https://docs.rs#2836)        assert!((zeta(2.0) - PI * PI / 6.0).abs() < 1e-12, "ζ(2)≠π²/6");
[2837](https://docs.rs#2837)        // ζ(4) = π⁴/90 (DLMF 25.6.2)
[2838](https://docs.rs#2838)        assert!((zeta(4.0) - PI.powi(4) / 90.0).abs() < 1e-12, "ζ(4)≠π⁴/90");
[2839](https://docs.rs#2839)        // ζ(0) = -1/2 (analytic continuation; DLMF 25.6.3)
[2840](https://docs.rs#2840)        assert!((zeta(0.0) - (-0.5)).abs() < 1e-14, "ζ(0)≠-½");
[2841](https://docs.rs#2841)        // ζ(-1) = -1/12 (DLMF 25.6.2; scipy fixture -0.0833...)
[2842](https://docs.rs#2842)        assert!((zeta(-1.0) - (-1.0 / 12.0)).abs() < 1e-12, "ζ(-1)≠-1/12");
[2843](https://docs.rs#2843)        // ζ(-2) = 0 (trivial zero at negative even integers; DLMF 25.4.2)
[2844](https://docs.rs#2844)        assert!(zeta(-2.0).abs() < 1e-13, "ζ(-2)≠0");
[2845](https://docs.rs#2845)        // ζ(3) = Apéry's constant ≈ 1.20206 (scipy fixture)
[2846](https://docs.rs#2846)        assert!((zeta(3.0) - 1.202_056_903_159_59).abs() < 1e-12, "ζ(3) Apéry");
[2847](https://docs.rs#2847)        // Pole: ζ(1) = NaN
[2848](https://docs.rs#2848)        assert!(zeta(1.0).is_nan(), "ζ(1) must be NaN (pole)");
[2849](https://docs.rs#2849)    }
[2850](https://docs.rs#2850)
[2851](https://docs.rs#2851)    // ── fresnel ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[2852](https://docs.rs#2852)
[2853](https://docs.rs#2853)    #[test]
[2854](https://docs.rs#2854)    fn fresnel_invariants_and_fixtures() {
[2855](https://docs.rs#2855)        // S(0)=C(0)=0 (trivial)
[2856](https://docs.rs#2856)        let (s0, c0) = fresnel(0.0);
[2857](https://docs.rs#2857)        assert_eq!((s0, c0), (0.0, 0.0));
[2858](https://docs.rs#2858)
[2859](https://docs.rs#2859)        // Odd-function symmetry: S(-x)=-S(x), C(-x)=-C(x)
[2860](https://docs.rs#2860)        for &x in &[0.5_f64, 1.0, 2.0] {
[2861](https://docs.rs#2861)            let (sp, cp) = fresnel(x);
[2862](https://docs.rs#2862)            let (sn, cn) = fresnel(-x);
[2863](https://docs.rs#2863)            assert!((sp + sn).abs() < 1e-14, "S not odd at x={x}");
[2864](https://docs.rs#2864)            assert!((cp + cn).abs() < 1e-14, "C not odd at x={x}");
[2865](https://docs.rs#2865)        }
[2866](https://docs.rs#2866)
[2867](https://docs.rs#2867)        // scipy 1.13 fixtures: convention S(x)=∫₀ˣ sin(πt²/2)dt, C(x)=∫₀ˣ cos(πt²/2)dt
[2868](https://docs.rs#2868)        let cases: &[(f64, f64, f64)] = &[
[2869](https://docs.rs#2869)            (0.5, 0.064_732_432_859_999_3, 0.492_344_225_871_446),
[2870](https://docs.rs#2870)            (1.0, 0.438_259_147_390_355, 0.779_893_400_376_823),
[2871](https://docs.rs#2871)            (2.0, 0.343_415_678_363_698, 0.488_253_406_075_341),
[2872](https://docs.rs#2872)            (5.0, 0.499_191_381_917_117, 0.563_631_188_704_012),
[2873](https://docs.rs#2873)        ];
[2874](https://docs.rs#2874)        for &(x, s_ref, c_ref) in cases {
[2875](https://docs.rs#2875)            let (s, c) = fresnel(x);
[2876](https://docs.rs#2876)            assert!((s - s_ref).abs() < 1e-11, "S({x})={s} ≠ {s_ref}");
[2877](https://docs.rs#2877)            assert!((c - c_ref).abs() < 1e-11, "C({x})={c} ≠ {c_ref}");
[2878](https://docs.rs#2878)        }
[2879](https://docs.rs#2879)
[2880](https://docs.rs#2880)        // Asymptotic: S(x)→1/2, C(x)→1/2. Oscillation bound: |S(x)-1/2| < 2/(π·x).
[2881](https://docs.rs#2881)        // At x=100: bound ≈ 0.00637. At x=5: bound ≈ 0.127 (looser but demonstrates trend).
[2882](https://docs.rs#2882)        for &x in &[20.0_f64, 50.0, 100.0] {
[2883](https://docs.rs#2883)            let (sx, _cx) = fresnel(x);
[2884](https://docs.rs#2884)            let bound = 2.0 / (std::f64::consts::PI * x) + 1e-10;
[2885](https://docs.rs#2885)            assert!((sx - 0.5).abs() <= bound, "S({x})={sx}, bound={bound}");
[2886](https://docs.rs#2886)        }
[2887](https://docs.rs#2887)    }
[2888](https://docs.rs#2888)
[2889](https://docs.rs#2889)    // ── hyp1f1 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[2890](https://docs.rs#2890)
[2891](https://docs.rs#2891)    #[test]
[2892](https://docs.rs#2892)    fn hyp1f1_closed_forms_and_fixtures() {
[2893](https://docs.rs#2893)        // ₁F₁(a;a;z) = eᶻ (DLMF 13.6.1)
[2894](https://docs.rs#2894)        let e = std::f64::consts::E;
[2895](https://docs.rs#2895)        assert!((hyp1f1(1.0, 1.0, 1.0).unwrap() - e).abs() < 1e-12,
[2896](https://docs.rs#2896)            "₁F₁(1;1;1)≠e");
[2897](https://docs.rs#2897)        assert!((hyp1f1(2.0, 2.0, -1.0).unwrap() - (-1.0_f64).exp()).abs() < 1e-12,
[2898](https://docs.rs#2898)            "₁F₁(2;2;-1)≠e⁻¹");
[2899](https://docs.rs#2899)
[2900](https://docs.rs#2900)        // ₁F₁(1;2;z) = (eᶻ−1)/z (DLMF 13.6.19)
[2901](https://docs.rs#2901)        let expected = (e - 1.0) / 1.0; // z=1 → (e-1)/1 = e-1
[2902](https://docs.rs#2902)        assert!((hyp1f1(1.0, 2.0, 1.0).unwrap() - expected).abs() < 1e-12,
[2903](https://docs.rs#2903)            "₁F₁(1;2;1)≠e−1");
[2904](https://docs.rs#2904)
[2905](https://docs.rs#2905)        // scipy 1.13 fixtures
[2906](https://docs.rs#2906)        assert!((hyp1f1(0.5, 1.5, 0.25).unwrap() - 1.089_974_208_367_24).abs() < 1e-11);
[2907](https://docs.rs#2907)        assert!((hyp1f1(2.0, 3.0, -1.0).unwrap() - 0.528_482_235_314_23).abs() < 1e-11);
[2908](https://docs.rs#2908)
[2909](https://docs.rs#2909)        // Domain: b non-positive integer → Err
[2910](https://docs.rs#2910)        assert!(hyp1f1(1.0, 0.0, 1.0).is_err());
[2911](https://docs.rs#2911)        assert!(hyp1f1(1.0, -1.0, 1.0).is_err());
[2912](https://docs.rs#2912)    }
[2913](https://docs.rs#2913)
[2914](https://docs.rs#2914)    // ── hyp2f1 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[2915](https://docs.rs#2915)
[2916](https://docs.rs#2916)    #[test]
[2917](https://docs.rs#2917)    fn hyp2f1_closed_forms_and_fixtures() {
[2918](https://docs.rs#2918)        // ₂F₁(1,1;2;z) = −ln(1−z)/z (DLMF 15.4.1)
[2919](https://docs.rs#2919)        // At z=0.5: −ln(0.5)/0.5 = ln(2)/0.5 = 2·ln(2)
[2920](https://docs.rs#2920)        let ln2 = std::f64::consts::LN_2;
[2921](https://docs.rs#2921)        assert!((hyp2f1(1.0, 1.0, 2.0, 0.5).unwrap() - 2.0 * ln2).abs() < 1e-12,
[2922](https://docs.rs#2922)            "₂F₁(1,1;2;0.5)≠2ln2");
[2923](https://docs.rs#2923)
[2924](https://docs.rs#2924)        // ₂F₁(a,b;b;z) = (1−z)^{−a} (DLMF 15.4.6)
[2925](https://docs.rs#2925)        assert!((hyp2f1(2.0, 3.0, 3.0, 0.5).unwrap() - 4.0).abs() < 1e-12,
[2926](https://docs.rs#2926)            "₂F₁(2,3;3;0.5)≠4");
[2927](https://docs.rs#2927)
[2928](https://docs.rs#2928)        // scipy 1.13 fixtures
[2929](https://docs.rs#2929)        // ₂F₁(½,½;³⁄₂;¼) = arcsin(½)/(½) = (π/6)/(½) = π/3 (closed form)
[2930](https://docs.rs#2930)        assert!((hyp2f1(0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 0.25).unwrap() - std::f64::consts::FRAC_PI_3).abs() < 1e-11);
[2931](https://docs.rs#2931)        assert!((hyp2f1(1.0, 2.0, 3.0, -0.5).unwrap() - 0.756_279_135_134_684).abs() < 1e-11);
[2932](https://docs.rs#2932)        assert!((hyp2f1(2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 0.3).unwrap() - 1.691_282_299_329_31).abs() < 1e-11);
[2933](https://docs.rs#2933)
[2934](https://docs.rs#2934)        // Domain: |z| >= 1 → Err
[2935](https://docs.rs#2935)        assert!(hyp2f1(1.0, 1.0, 2.0, 1.0).is_err());
[2936](https://docs.rs#2936)        assert!(hyp2f1(1.0, 1.0, 2.0, -1.5).is_err());
[2937](https://docs.rs#2937)        // c non-positive integer → Err
[2938](https://docs.rs#2938)        assert!(hyp2f1(1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.5).is_err());
[2939](https://docs.rs#2939)    }

[2965](https://docs.rs#2965)    fn struve_h_minus_half_closed_form() {

[2972](https://docs.rs#2972)            "H_{{-1/2}}(1) = {got}, expected {expected}");

[3018](https://docs.rs#3018)    #[test]
[3019](https://docs.rs#3019)    fn struve_h_asymptotic_half_plus() {
[3020](https://docs.rs#3020)        // H_{1/2}(21) via asymptotic branch (x > 20 threshold).
[3021](https://docs.rs#3021)        // Oracle: closed form H_{1/2}(x) = √(2/(πx))(1−cos x).
[3022](https://docs.rs#3022)        use std::f64::consts::PI;
[3023](https://docs.rs#3023)        let x = 21.0_f64;
[3024](https://docs.rs#3024)        let expected = (2.0 / (PI * x)).sqrt() * (1.0 - x.cos());

[3026](https://docs.rs#3026)        assert!((got - expected).abs() < 1e-8,
[3027](https://docs.rs#3027)            "H_{{1/2}}(21) = {got}, expected {expected}");

[3031](https://docs.rs#3031)    fn struve_h_asymptotic_half_minus() {
[3032](https://docs.rs#3032)        // H_{-1/2}(21): asymptotic correction = 0 exactly (1/Γ(0)=0),
[3033](https://docs.rs#3033)        // so struve_h delegates to bessel_yv(−½, 21) ≈ √(2/(πx)) sin x.
[3034](https://docs.rs#3034)        // Tolerance accounts for bessel_yv accuracy (~1e-8).
[3035](https://docs.rs#3035)        use std::f64::consts::PI;
[3036](https://docs.rs#3036)        let x = 21.0_f64;
[3037](https://docs.rs#3037)        let expected = (2.0 / (PI * x)).sqrt() * x.sin();
[3038](https://docs.rs#3038)        let got = struve_h(-0.5, x);
[3039](https://docs.rs#3039)        assert!((got - expected).abs() < 1e-7,
[3040](https://docs.rs#3040)            "H_{{-1/2}}(21) = {got}, expected {expected}");
[3041](https://docs.rs#3041)    }

[3095](https://docs.rs#3095)        let u = 0.73_f64;
[3096](https://docs.rs#3096)        let (sn0, cn0, dn0, _) = ellipj(u, 0.0);
[3097](https://docs.rs#3097)        assert!((sn0 - u.sin()).abs() < 1e-12);
[3098](https://docs.rs#3098)        assert!((cn0 - u.cos()).abs() < 1e-12);

[3105](https://docs.rs#3105)

[3107](https://docs.rs#3107)        let (sn, cn, dn, _) = ellipj(u, m);
[3108](https://docs.rs#3108)        assert!((sn * sn + cn * cn - 1.0).abs() < 1e-10);
[3109](https://docs.rs#3109)        assert!((dn * dn + m * sn * sn - 1.0).abs() < 1e-10);
[3110](https://docs.rs#3110)    }

[3138](https://docs.rs#3138)
[3139](https://docs.rs#3139)    #[test]
[3140](https://docs.rs#3140)    fn test_airy_taylor_region() {
[3141](https://docs.rs#3141)        // Taylor series region |x| <= 5
[3142](https://docs.rs#3142)        // Ai(1): NIST DLMF Table 9.12
[3143](https://docs.rs#3143)        let (ai1, aip1) = airy::airy_ai(1.0);
[3144](https://docs.rs#3144)        assert!((ai1 - 0.135_292_416_312_88).abs() < 1e-10, "Ai(1) = {ai1}");
[3145](https://docs.rs#3145)        // Derivative convergence limited by fp_num/x accumulation: 1e-8 is sufficient
[3146](https://docs.rs#3146)        assert!(
[3147](https://docs.rs#3147)            (aip1 - (-0.159_147_446_167_14)).abs() < 1e-7,
[3148](https://docs.rs#3148)            "Ai'(1) = {aip1}"
[3149](https://docs.rs#3149)        );
[3150](https://docs.rs#3150)
[3151](https://docs.rs#3151)        // Wronskian Ai·Bi' − Ai'·Bi = 1/π (exact identity, NIST DLMF 9.2.8)
[3152](https://docs.rs#3152)        // Follows from Abel's theorem for y''=xy: any two solutions have constant Wronskian.
[3153](https://docs.rs#3153)        let pi_inv = 1.0 / std::f64::consts::PI;
[3154](https://docs.rs#3154)        for &x in &[0.0, 1.0, -1.0, 2.5, -3.0, -5.0, 5.0] {
[3155](https://docs.rs#3155)            let (ai, aip) = airy::airy_ai(x);
[3156](https://docs.rs#3156)            let (bi, bip) = airy::airy_bi(x);
[3157](https://docs.rs#3157)            let w = ai * bip - aip * bi;
[3158](https://docs.rs#3158)            assert!((w - pi_inv).abs() < 1e-10, "Wronskian at x={x}: {w}");
[3159](https://docs.rs#3159)        }
[3160](https://docs.rs#3160)    }
[3161](https://docs.rs#3161)
[3162](https://docs.rs#3162)    #[test]
[3163](https://docs.rs#3163)    fn test_airy_asymptotic_region() {
[3164](https://docs.rs#3164)        let pi_inv = 1.0 / std::f64::consts::PI;
[3165](https://docs.rs#3165)        // Wronskian Ai·Bi' − Ai'·Bi = 1/π; tolerance reflects Olver series truncation error:
[3166](https://docs.rs#3166)        //   x=±6:  ζ≈9.8,  ~3 even + ~2 odd terms, error O(1e-3)
[3167](https://docs.rs#3167)        //   x=±10: ζ≈21,   ~6 terms, error O(1e-4)
[3168](https://docs.rs#3168)        //   x=±20: ζ≈60,   ~9 terms, error O(1e-5) — residuals compound in product
[3169](https://docs.rs#3169)        for &(x, tol) in &[
[3170](https://docs.rs#3170)            (6.0_f64, 1e-3),
[3171](https://docs.rs#3171)            (-6.0, 1e-3),
[3172](https://docs.rs#3172)            (10.0, 5e-4),
[3173](https://docs.rs#3173)            (-10.0, 5e-4),
[3174](https://docs.rs#3174)            (20.0, 5e-5),
[3175](https://docs.rs#3175)            (-20.0, 5e-5),
[3176](https://docs.rs#3176)        ] {
[3177](https://docs.rs#3177)            let (ai, aip) = airy::airy_ai(x);
[3178](https://docs.rs#3178)            let (bi, bip) = airy::airy_bi(x);
[3179](https://docs.rs#3179)            let w = ai * bip - aip * bi;
[3180](https://docs.rs#3180)            assert!(
[3181](https://docs.rs#3181)                (w - pi_inv).abs() < tol,
[3182](https://docs.rs#3182)                "Wronskian at x={x}: got {w}, want {pi_inv}±{tol}"
[3183](https://docs.rs#3183)            );
[3184](https://docs.rs#3184)        }
[3185](https://docs.rs#3185)    }

# beta in yatrosci_special::gamma_funcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/gamma_funcs/fn.beta.html

## Expand description

Compute the beta function `B(a, b)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

`B(a, b) = \frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}`Computed efficiently via log-gamma to avoid overflow: `\exp(\ln\Gamma(a) + \ln\Gamma(b) - \ln\Gamma(a+b))`.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §5.12.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)

---

# betainc in yatrosci_special::gamma_funcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/gamma_funcs/fn.betainc.html

## Expand description

Compute the regularized incomplete beta function `I_x(a, b)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

`I_x(a, b) = \frac{1}{B(a, b)} \int_0^x t^{a-1} (1-t)^{b-1} dt`Uses a continued fraction expansion with Lentz’s method. Symmetry `I_x(a,b) = 1 - I_{1-x}(b,a)`
is applied to ensure rapid convergence.

[§](https://docs.rs#precisi%C3%B3n-num%C3%A9rica)Precisión numérica

Converges typically in less than 100 iterations. Tiny values `1e-30` used to prevent division by zero in Lentz’s method.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §8.17.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)
- Abramowitz, M., & Stegun, I. A. (1964). *Handbook of Mathematical Functions*. Eq 26.5.8.
- Press, W. H., et al. (2007). *Numerical Recipes*. §6.4.

---

# betaln in yatrosci_special::gamma_funcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/gamma_funcs/fn.betaln.html

## Expand description

Compute the logarithm of the beta function, `\ln(B(a, b))`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

`\ln B(a, b) = \ln\Gamma(a) + \ln\Gamma(b) - \ln\Gamma(a+b)`[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §5.12.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)

---

# binom in yatrosci_special::gamma_funcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/gamma_funcs/fn.binom.html

## Expand description

Compute the binomial coefficient `C(n, k)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

`\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}`Computed analytically using logarithmic gamma expressions for large arguments.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §1.2.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)

# digamma in yatrosci_special::gamma_funcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/gamma_funcs/fn.digamma.html

## Expand description

Compute the digamma function (psi function), `\psi(x)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

`\psi(x) = \frac{d}{dx} \ln(\Gamma(x)) = \frac{\Gamma'(x)}{\Gamma(x)}`Uses asymptotic expansion for `x > 10`, recurrence relation for `x < 1`,
reflection formula for negative `x`, and series expansion otherwise.

[§](https://docs.rs#precisi%C3%B3n-num%C3%A9rica)Precisión numérica

- Asymptotic expansion for large `x`uses Bernoulli numbers up to 6th order.
- Truncation at 100 iterations for series expansion.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §5.11.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)
- Abramowitz, M., & Stegun, I. A. (1964). *Handbook of Mathematical Functions*. Eq 6.3.18.

---

[Source](../../src/yatrosci_special/lib.rs.html#500-506) `pub fn factorial(n: `[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)) -> [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)

# gamma in yatrosci_special::gamma_funcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/gamma_funcs/fn.gamma.html

## Expand description

Compute the gamma function `Gamma(x)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

`\Gamma(x) = \int_0^\infty t^{x-1} e^{-t} dt`Uses the Lanczos approximation internally via the `libm` crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#precisi%C3%B3n-num%C3%A9rica)Precisión numérica

Relies on `libm::tgamma` which provides close to IEEE 754 double precision.
Returns `NaN` for non-positive integers.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §5.2.1.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)
- Abramowitz, M., & Stegun, I. A. (1964). *Handbook of Mathematical Functions*. §6.1.

[§](https://docs.rs#advertencias-num%C3%A9ricas)Advertencias numéricas

Has poles at non-positive integers where it returns `NaN` instead of infinity to avoid silent propagation of unbounded values.

---

# gammainc in yatrosci_special::gamma_funcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/gamma_funcs/fn.gammainc.html

## Expand description

Compute the lower regularized incomplete gamma function `P(a, x)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

`P(a, x) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(a)} \int_0^x t^{a-1} e^{-t} dt`Uses series expansion for `x < a + 1` and continued fractions for `x \ge a + 1`.

[§](https://docs.rs#precisi%C3%B3n-num%C3%A9rica)Precisión numérica

Maximum 100 iterations. Truncation tolerance `1e-10`.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §8.2.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)
- Press, W. H., et al. (2007). *Numerical Recipes*. §6.2.

---

# gammaincc in yatrosci_special::gamma_funcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/gamma_funcs/fn.gammaincc.html

## Expand description

Compute the upper regularized incomplete gamma function `Q(a, x)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

`Q(a, x) = 1 - P(a, x) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(a)} \int_x^\infty t^{a-1} e^{-t} dt`[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §8.2.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)

# lgamma in yatrosci_special::gamma_funcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/gamma_funcs/fn.lgamma.html

## Expand description

Compute the natural logarithm of the gamma function, `\ln(\Gamma(x))`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

Delegates to `libm::lgamma`.

[§](https://docs.rs#precisi%C3%B3n-num%C3%A9rica)Precisión numérica

Avoids the overflow that would occur if computing `gamma(x).ln()` for large `x`.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

# erf in yatrosci_special::erf_funcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/erf_funcs/fn.erf.html

## Expand description

Compute the error function `erf(x)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

`\text{erf}(x) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_0^x e^{-t^2} dt`Delegates to `libm::erf`.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §7.2.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)

# erfc in yatrosci_special::erf_funcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/erf_funcs/fn.erfc.html

## Expand description

Compute the complementary error function `erfc(x)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

`\text{erfc}(x) = 1 - \text{erf}(x) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_x^\infty e^{-t^2} dt`Delegates to `libm::erfc`. Numerically stable for large `x`.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §7.2.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)

---

# erfcinv in yatrosci_special::erf_funcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/erf_funcs/fn.erfcinv.html

## Expand description

Compute the inverse complementary error function `erfcinv(y)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

Evaluated simply as `erfinv(1 - y)`. Note that precision may degrade for values of `y` extremely close to 0.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- Cody, W. J. (1969). Rational Chebyshev Approximations for the Error Function.
DOI: [10.1090/S0025-5718-1969-0240954-4](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1969-0240954-4)

# erfcx in yatrosci_special::erf_funcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/erf_funcs/fn.erfcx.html

## Expand description

Compute the scaled complementary error function `erfcx(x)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

`\text{erfcx}(x) = e^{x^2} \text{erfc}(x)`[§](https://docs.rs#precisi%C3%B3n-num%C3%A9rica)Precisión numérica

Uses an asymptotic expansion `1 / (x \sqrt{\pi})` for `x > 26.0` to avoid `NaN` caused by multiplying extremely large `e^{x^2}` with extremely small `erfc(x)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §7.2.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)

---

# erfinv in yatrosci_special::erf_funcs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/erf_funcs/fn.erfinv.html

## Expand description

Compute the inverse error function `erfinv(y)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

Returns `x` such that `erf(x) = y`.
Uses a rational Chebyshev approximation for evaluation.

[§](https://docs.rs#precisi%C3%B3n-num%C3%A9rica)Precisión numérica

The polynomial coefficients are derived from rational Chebyshev approximations, achieving near machine precision.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- Cody, W. J. (1969). Rational Chebyshev Approximations for the Error Function.
*Mathematics of Computation*, 23(107), 631-638. DOI:[10.1090/S0025-5718-1969-0240954-4](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1969-0240954-4)

---

# i0 in yatrosci_special::bessel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/bessel/fn.i0.html

## Expand description

Compute the modified Bessel function of the first kind, order 0, `I_0(x)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

Evaluated using piecewise polynomial approximations divided at `|x| = 3.75`.

[§](https://docs.rs#precisi%C3%B3n-num%C3%A9rica)Precisión numérica

The polynomial coefficients are standard minimax approximations yielding precision up to `1e-7` to `1e-8`.
See Abramowitz & Stegun Eq. 9.8.1 and 9.8.2.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- Abramowitz, M., & Stegun, I. A. (1964). *Handbook of Mathematical Functions*. Eqs. 9.8.1 - 9.8.2.
- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §10.25.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)

---

# iv in yatrosci_special::bessel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/bessel/fn.iv.html

## Expand description

Compute the modified Bessel function of the first kind, real order `\nu`, `I_\nu(x)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

Evaluated using a series expansion for non-integer configurations.

[§](https://docs.rs#precisi%C3%B3n-num%C3%A9rica)Precisión numérica

# jv in yatrosci_special::bessel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/bessel/fn.jv.html

## Expand description

Compute the Bessel function of the first kind, real order `\nu`, `J_\nu(x)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

If `\nu` is integer, delegates to `jn`. Otherwise, computes via a Maclaurin series expansion.

[§](https://docs.rs#precisi%C3%B3n-num%C3%A9rica)Precisión numérica

The series expansion converges well for small to moderate `x`. It evaluates up to 100 terms until relative correction drops below `1e-15`.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §10.2.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)

---

# yv in yatrosci_special::bessel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/bessel/fn.yv.html

## Expand description

Compute the Bessel function of the second kind, real order `\nu`, `Y_\nu(x)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

Evaluated using the standard identity:

`Y_\nu(x) = \frac{J_\nu(x) \cos(\nu\pi) - J_{-\nu}(x)}{\sin(\nu\pi)}`[§](https://docs.rs#precisi%C3%B3n-num%C3%A9rica)Precisión numérica

Suffers from catastrophic cancellation if `\nu` is close to an integer. However, the logic handles exact integers explicitly.

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §10.2.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)

---

# ellipe in yatrosci_special::elliptic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/elliptic/fn.ellipe.html

## Expand description

Compute the complete elliptic integral of the second kind `E(m)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

`E(m) = \int_0^{\pi/2} \sqrt{1 - m \sin^2(t)} dt`Evaluated using the Arithmetic-Geometric Mean (AGM) sequence combined with a summation property.

[§](https://docs.rs#precisi%C3%B3n-num%C3%A9rica)Precisión numérica

AGM iterates until `c_n < 1e-15` (up to 30 iterations).

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §19.8.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)

---

# ellipeinc in yatrosci_special::elliptic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/elliptic/fn.ellipeinc.html

## Expand description

Compute the incomplete elliptic integral of the second kind `E(\phi, m)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

Expressed in terms of Carlson’s symmetric forms `R_F` and `R_D`.

`E(\phi, m) = \sin(\phi) R_F(...) - \frac{m}{3} \sin^3(\phi) R_D(...)`[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- Carlson, B. C. (1995). Numerical computation of real or complex elliptic integrals.
*Numerical Algorithms*, 10(1), 13-26. DOI:[10.1007/BF02198293](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02198293)

---

# ellipf in yatrosci_special::elliptic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/elliptic/fn.ellipf.html

## Expand description

Compute the incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind `F(\phi, m)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

Expressed in terms of Carlson’s symmetric form `R_F`.

`F(\phi, m) = \sin(\phi) R_F(\cos^2\phi, 1 - m\sin^2\phi, 1)`[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- Carlson, B. C. (1995). Numerical computation of real or complex elliptic integrals.
*Numerical Algorithms*, 10(1), 13-26. DOI:[10.1007/BF02198293](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02198293)

---

# ellipj in yatrosci_special::elliptic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/elliptic/fn.ellipj.html

## Expand description

Compute Jacobi elliptic functions `(sn(u|m), cn(u|m), dn(u|m), am(u|m))`.

REF: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §22.2 and §22.20 https://dlmf.nist.gov/22 REF: Carlson, B. C. (1995) “Numerical computation of real or complex elliptic integrals” DOI: 10.1007/BF02198293 Peer-reviewed: Numerical Algorithms, ISSN 1017-1398 Validado contra: casos m=0, m=1 e identidades sn^2+cn^2=1, dn^2+m sn^2=1.

# ellipk in yatrosci_special::elliptic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-special/0.1.0/yatrosci_special/elliptic/fn.ellipk.html

## Expand description

Compute the complete elliptic integral of the first kind `K(m)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#algoritmo)Algoritmo

`K(m) = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - m \sin^2(t)}} dt`Evaluated using the Arithmetic-Geometric Mean (AGM) method.

[§](https://docs.rs#precisi%C3%B3n-num%C3%A9rica)Precisión numérica

AGM iterates until consecutive means converge within `1e-15` (up to 30 iterations).

[§](https://docs.rs#referencias)Referencias

- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. §19.8.
DOI: [10.6028/jres.069b.001](https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.069b.001)
